question: According to the European Centre for Disease Control (ECDC), the EU agency responsible for pandemics, around 1.5 billion doses have been delivered and 1 billion doses have been injected1. That would therefore mean that around 500 million doses have not been used directly, including 100 million in France (figures as of 5 October 2023, no update since then).

Unlike Italy, France seems to have received many more vaccines than it has used: 260 million doses have reportedly been delivered but just 160 million have been administered, which is a potential waste of 100 million vaccines. Italy appears to have wasted 14 times fewer jabs than France: only 7 million doses have been delivered but not administered.
According to Politico, 215 million doses – worth EUR 4 billion – are known to have been thrown away in Europe.2 1.
Has the Commission verified the ECDC figures and can it confirm that the difference in the number of doses distributed and administered is 100 million for France?
Does the ECDC base its information on figures provided by the Commission, France or the manufacturers?
How does the Commission explain the ECDC’s seemingly inconsistent figures for Denmark: 15 million jabs administered but just 9 million delivered?

According to the ECDC, 1 485 522 082 doses have been supplied and 981 410 200 doses have been administered within the EU/EEA; in France, 260 480 930 doses have been distributed and 160 412 817 administered; in Italy, 157 million doses have been distributed and 150 million administered. France refused to reply to Politico.

‘If this average waste rate is projected across the rest of the EU, it would equal more than 312 million destroyed vaccines.’ https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-bonfire-covidvaccines-coronavirus-waste-europe-analysis.
answer: The primary objective of the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) COVID-19 Vaccine Tracker was to provide a rapid overview of the progress in the roll-out of COVID-19 vaccines across EU/European Economic Area (EEA) countries during some of the most critical months of the pandemic.

EU/EEA countries have been reporting data to the ECDC based on information available at the national level at the time of submission. However, such data is only available up to specific cut-off dates and points in time, depending on the national context, and can no longer be considered up to date. The ECDC no longer collects data on vaccine doses distributed.

As a result, the most accurate and up-to-date figures on vaccines provided by manufacturers should be requested to the relevant national competent authorities. The ECDC continues to collect data on vaccine coverage in order to assess the level of uptake of COVID-19 vaccines in the most vulnerable target groups for vaccination during the winter season (3).

In the specific case of Denmark, the Danish authorities issued a disclaimer (4) at the time of data submission to the ECDC regarding potential discrepancies in the figures. Generally, it is not surprising to see the number of vaccine doses distributed or purchased exceed the number of vaccines administered.

The future demand for vaccines can be estimated in advance but it will always entail a degree of uncertainty at the time of procurement, in particular in situations where uncertainty exists about the development of the epidemiological situation.

According to the ECDC, 1 485 522 082 doses have been supplied and 981 410 200 doses have been administered within the EU/EEA; in France, 260 480 930 doses have been distributed and 160 412 817 administered; in Italy, 157 million doses have been distributed and 150 million administered. France refused to reply to Politico.

‘If this average waste rate is projected across the rest of the EU, it would equal more than 312 million destroyed vaccines.’ https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-bonfire-covid-vaccines-coronavirus-waste-europe-analysis. The latest report in this regard is available at: https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/sites/default/files/documents/interim-vaccine-overage-eu-eea-2023-24.
